newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albanian police crack down on gangster scourge.
newsitem.headline: Albanian police crack down on gangster scourge.

text.p: Police in Albania said on Tuesday they had launched a big crackdown on gangsterism to restore law and order after months of unrest sparked by the collapse of investment pyramid schemes.

Sources in the Interior Ministry said special unit forces entered the chaotic southern towns of Vlore, Gjirokaster, Sarande and Tepelene, which have been under the control of heavily-armed gangs since March.
"Police forces are determined to act with firmness against eventual resistence by armed gangs," one source said.

Haxhi Demiri, police chief in Vlore, 145 km (90 miles) southwest of Tirana, told Reuters police had been ferreting out gangsters since Sunday night in a bid to bring the violence-stricken port back under their control.
"So far we have arrested three criminals who are members of Zani's band," Demiri said in reference to mob boss Lefter Zani, also known as Vlore's most wanted man.

Zani told the leading daily Koha Jone newspaper on Tuesday he would avenge the police action. "We have some 40,000 people with more than 25,000 guns, bombs and grenades....We will fight until former president Sali Berisha is hanged in Vlore's main square," he said.

Berisha is especially hated in southern Albania for allowing bogus investment funds to flourish before collapsing, costing many people their life savings. His party was trounced in general elections six weeks ago.

A Vlore resident told Reuters he saw scores of policemen in bullet-proof vests surround the Cole area where Zani had taken refuge. Meanwhile, other police forces had taken full control of the road linking Vlore to the northern town of Fieri.
"We cannot afford to let such criminals walk free and we are determined to put an end to this pessimistic situation which has made Vlore a real cemetery," police chief Demiri said.
More than 1,500 people have been killed in Europe's most impoverished country since violence, lawlessness and looting broke out in March after the demise of the pyramid investment schemes.

Berisha's Democratic Party government was forced to resign. An interim 10-party government led the country to the June 29 election, which was overwhelmingly won by a leftist coalition led by the Socialists.

The international community, which helped Albania stage the elections, has made clear it will continue assistance if the ruling coalition restores order, improves human rights and adopts sound economic policies.
